cut_items.item: Distinguish leak vs. limit too low: heap rises and falls but peaks near limit means limit is too low
Use --heapsnapshot-near-heap-limit=3 to write a snapshot just before the crash for production evidence
Run under a process manager (PM2, systemd, Kubernetes) so the service restarts after a crash
Warning: do not expose --inspect on a public port
MaxListenersExceededWarning as a signal for listener leaks
Unbounded queues or streams without backpressure when producer outpaces consumer
Per-request data attached to long-lived objects, e.g. DB connection or high-cardinality metrics labels
Use an LRU cache with a max size as the fix for unbounded caches
Closures that keep large objects alive

added_items.item: Heap snapshots pause the process and can need about 2x heap memory, so take them on one instance, not all of production
If the heap looks stable but the process dies, check non-heap memory (rss, external, Buffers, native addons), which does not appear in heap snapshots
Use the Retainers view to see what holds the growing objects
Take snapshots at start, after 1 hour and after 2 hours (a concrete schedule)
Tools clinic.js (clinic heapprofiler) and memlab as alternatives to hand-reading snapshots
Restart the service on a schedule as a stopgap
--max-old-space-size value is in MB; default depends on Node version and system memory
Without a container limit lower than the heap, the kernel OOM-kills (OOMKilled) before Node can report an error
Large request/response bodies held in memory instead of streamed
Unclosed resources such as DB connections, sockets, streams
Libraries with known leaks; check their issue trackers
Final step: fix the cause then confirm heapUsed stays flat
chrome://inspect as the way to connect DevTools to --inspect
